Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] IIS web shell (w3wp.exe) spawning recon, curl exfil, or RAR staging · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CL-STA-1062 Targets Southeast Asian Governments and Critical Infrastructure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TinyRCT backdoor masquerading as PerfWatson2.exe executing from %LOCALAPPDATA% · [LLM] Scheduled task persistence for GoogleUpdater or VMware-disguised VNT binary · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT C2 and tool-staging infrastructure · [LLM] SoftEther VPN / VNT tunneler masquerading as VMware vmtools.exe · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Password-protected RAR staging of data for exfiltration (-hp) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
TinyRCT backdoor masquerading as PerfWatson2.exe executing from %LOCALAPPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 TinyRCT .NET backdoor, which masquerades as Visual Studio's PerfWatson2.exe but enforces an environment check that it runs only from %LOCALAPPDATA%. Legitimate PerfWatson2.exe ships inside the Visual Studio install tree under Program Files, so any PerfWatson2.exe launching from AppData\Local is article-specific TinyRCT behaviour. Rationale: Uses the article's exact masquerade name PerfWatson2.exe plus TinyRCT's own self-imposed %LOCALAPPDATA% execution constraint; legitimate PerfWatson2 lives under Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio, making AppData\Local execution near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1497.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a portable/extracted copy of Visual Studio components from a profile folder
  • Visual Studio installer caching PerfWatson2 in AppData during an update (rare, usually Program Files)
  • Security tooling copying the binary to AppData for analysis on an analyst workstation
  • EDR sandbox detonation copying the sample into LocalAppData
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" and not(FolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and confirm it is not the signed Microsoft PerfWatson2 (legit is signed 'Microsoft Corporation' under Program Files). Check the parent process and whether the host concurrently beaconed to 45.32.113.172 or 139.180.134.221. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the AppData\Local copy; block both C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search the environment for any PerfWatson2.exe outside Program Files, for the GoogleUpdater scheduled task, and for choice.exe-based self-delete batch chains indicating TinyRCT cleanup.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "PerfWatson2.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\PerfWatson2.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection to CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT C2 and tool-staging infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the two confirmed CL-STA-1062 IPs: 45.32.113.172 (TinyRCT HTTP C2, ~10s beacon) and 139.180.134.221 (payload/tool-staging server hosting the PerfWatson2.exe backdoor and RAR tool archives). Pure-IOC network detection for both beaconing and payload pull. Rationale: Both IPs are explicitly named in the article (139.180.134.221 hosting PerfWatson2.exe; 45.32.113.172 as TinyRCT C2 in the kill-chain block) and confirmed across the Unit 42 report and Talos UAT-7237 overlap; raw IOC hits are high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or sandbox sandboxing the sample and reaching the C2
  • Threat-intel scanning/validation services probing the IPs from a corporate range
  • Shared Vultr/cloud hosting reassigning the IP to a benign tenant after takedown (verify timestamps against report publication)
  • Internal vuln scanner configured to crawl flagged IOCs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process; if it is PerfWatson2.exe, a fake vmtools.exe, or curl.exe from a web-server context, treat as confirmed. Note beacon cadence (~10s = TinyRCT). 2) Contain: block both IPs at firewall/proxy, isolate the source host, and capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on src_ip for prior 139.180.134.221 downloads (RAR/SoftEther tool pulls), and sweep all hosts for second-stage payloads delivered from the staging server.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SoftEther VPN / VNT tunneler masquerading as VMware vmtools.exe AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts CL-STA-1062's habit of disguising tunneling tools (SoftEther VPN, VNT) as VMware system binaries such as vmtools.exe. Flags processes named vmtools/vmtoolsd whose signing company is not 'VMware, Inc.' or whose product string references SoftEther — i.e. a VMware-named binary that isn't VMware. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's Figure 6/7 masquerade (SoftEther disguised as vmtools.exe, VNT disguised as a VMware executable); the company-name/path mismatch separates the tunneler from genuine VMware Tools without needing a hash. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine VMware Tools where version metadata is stripped/empty after repackaging by an MSP
  • Older VMware Tools builds signed under a legacy company string ('VMware, Inc.' variations)
  • Third-party VM management tools legitimately named vmtools running from a non-standard path
  • Software-distribution systems staging VMware Tools in a temp folder before install
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\VMware\VMware Tools\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the binary's digital signature and the command line for SoftEther/VNT tunnel arguments (server address, listen port). Confirm it isn't VMware-signed. 2) Contain: terminate the tunneler, isolate the host, and block its configured remote VPN/relay endpoint. 3) Hunt: look for scheduled tasks launching the same disguised binary, RDP sessions riding the tunnel, and the same masquerade name on peer hosts indicating lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "VMware, Inc." or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "SoftEther"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ActingProcessFileCompany != "VMware, Inc." or ActingProcessFileProduct has "SoftEther"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessFileProduct, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: VMware vmtools.exe Name Masquerade by Non-VMware Binary (SoftEther/VNT)
id: c7e3a915-44d8-4b62-9f0a-1d6c8e2b3a47

Scheduled task persistence for GoogleUpdater or VMware-disguised VNT binary AIInstallation Medium
Detects CL-STA-1062 establishing persistence via schtasks.exe creating a task named GoogleUpdater (TinyRCT loader) or a task launching a tunneler disguised as vmtools/VNT (Figure 7). Pivots on the task-creation command line rather than the binary itself. Rationale: Combines the article/kill-chain GoogleUpdater task name (TinyRCT loader) with the Figure 7 VNT-as-VMware scheduled task; task creation referencing these masquerade tokens is far more specific than generic schtasks alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Google Chrome/Updater creating GoogleUpdateTaskMachineCore tasks (note: name differs from 'GoogleUpdater')
  • VMware Tools installer registering a legitimate vmtools-related task
  • Admin scripts re-creating VMware service tasks during template provisioning
  • Software-packaging tools that template task names containing 'vmtools'
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\VMware\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task action (the binary path and arguments the task launches) and verify whether it points to a signed Google/VMware binary in its standard location. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task, isolate the host, and quarantine the referenced binary. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks across the fleet for the same name/binary, and correlate the task creator process — if it was a web shell (w3wp.exe) or PerfWatson2.exe, escalate to full IR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Creation for GoogleUpdater or VMware-Disguised Tunneler

IIS web shell (w3wp.exe) spawning recon, curl exfil, or RAR staging AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 ASPX web-shell command-execution channel where the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns cmd/curl/rar and native recon binaries — the actor piped system/network enumeration to actor IPs via curl and staged source code into RAR archives directly from the web shell. Rationale: Encodes the article's web-shell-as-execution-mechanism (Figure 4 curl enumeration, Figure 2 source-code archiving) via the w3wp.exe parent pivot — IIS workers should virtually never spawn curl, rar, tracert, or whoami. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web applications shelling out to net.exe/whoami for diagnostics
  • Application deployment scripts invoking cmd.exe under the app pool identity
  • Monitoring agents that run ipconfig/netstat from a web context
  • Developer health-check endpoints that exec systeminfo
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck", "\\Monitoring\\") and FileName in~ ("ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command lines — recon piped to curl targeting 45.32.113.172/139.180.134.221 or rar with -hp confirms malicious use; review IIS logs for the requesting URI and source IP (the web shell). 2) Contain: pull the offending .aspx file, isolate the web server, and reset the app-pool service account credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate recently written/modified .aspx files in web roots, and pivot on the source IP across other internet-facing servers for the same web-shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe", "httpd.exe", "php-cgi.exe", "tomcat.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "curl.exe", "rar.exe", "whoami.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "tracert.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "netstat.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\curl.exe", @"\rar.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\ipconfig.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\tracert.exe", @"\systeminfo.exe", @"\netstat.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Password-protected RAR staging of data for exfiltration (-hp) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CL-STA-1062's data-staging step: compressing findings (MSSQL dumps, entire web-server source-code directories) into header-encrypted, password-protected RAR archives using the rar -hp flag prior to exfil. Pivots on the -hp<password> add-to-archive command line, which survives binary renaming. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit tradecraft of compressing findings into password-protected RAR archives; the -hp<password> token (header encryption with an inline password) is rarely used by legitimate users and is the actor's recurring staging signature. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admins archiving log bundles or backups with a password for transport
  • Legitimate use of WinRAR with -hp by a power user securing personal data
  • Backup software that wraps RAR with header encryption
  • Developers packaging release artifacts with a protected archive
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Backup\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the archive path and contents source — large archives built from web roots, database export folders, or user document trees signal staging. Check which process invoked rar (web shell = high severity). 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the archive, and watch for immediate outbound transfer to the actor IPs. 3) Hunt: correlate the archive creation time with subsequent curl/POST egress and SoftEther tunnel activity; sweep peer hosts for the same -hp pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-hp\S+"
| where ProcessCommandLine has " a "
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-hp\S+"
| where CommandLine has " a "
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

description: |

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Beyond IOCs: AI-enabled threat intelligence
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Prototype-pollution payload (__proto__/constructor.prototype) in HTTP request to i18next missing-key route AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound web requests carrying prototype-pollution key tokens ("__proto__", "constructor.prototype") that abuse i18next-fs-backend ≤2.6.5's missing-key persistence (CVE-2026-48713) to walk into Object.prototype. Article-specific because it keys on the exact dotted-segment strings the setPath/getLastOfPath walker fails to guard, delivered via untrusted request bodies to a saveMissing route. Rationale: Uses the exact unsafe segments the article names as unguarded in getLastOfPath ("__proto__", "constructor", "prototype") split on the default "." keySeparator; "__proto__" and "constructor.prototype" in a request URI are extremely rare in benign traffic, so this is high-fidelity for the delivery of the pollution payload. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2933-q333-qg83 • https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-middleware/security/advisories/GHSA-f49m-vf83-692w
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated DAST / prototype-pollution scanners (Burp, Nuclei, ZAP) probing the app
  • Authorized penetration test or bug-bounty researcher testing the missingKeyHandler route
  • Security-training or CTF traffic replaying prototype-pollution payloads
  • Legitimate app that genuinely uses a translation key literally named 'constructor' (rare, benign)
  • Log-replay / traffic-mirroring tooling re-sending historical malicious requests
Suppression filter
| where UA !has_any ("Nuclei","nikto","ZAP","sqlmap","Burp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (method, path, body if WAF captures it) and confirm it targets an i18next missing-key / saveMissing route; check the source IP's request history for scanner user-agents vs. a single targeted hit. 2) Contain: if the app runs i18next-fs-backend ≤2.6.5 with missingKeyHandler exposed to untrusted input, block the source IP at the WAF and apply a workaround (mount the route behind auth, set saveMissing:false, or keySeparator:false) pending upgrade to 2.6.6. 3) Hunt: search other web logs for the same source IP and for additional pollution tokens; inspect written locale/translation JSON files for injected __proto__/constructor keys and review the Node process for crashes or corrupted config after the request.

Attack-surface hunt surfacing endpoints where Defender/Sentinel TVM has inventoried i18next-fs-backend below the fixed 2.6.6 release. Article-specific: keys on the exact package name and CVE so SOC/vuln-mgmt can prioritise upgrade or workaround on internet-reachable Node apps. Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE-2026-48713 and package name i18next-fs-backend named in the advisory; the fix is 2.6.6 so any inventoried version below that on a reachable host is a direct exposure to the prototype-pollution path. Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Response runbook

i18next-http-middleware dotted prototype-pollution key in HTTP request (CVE-2026-48714) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound web requests carrying a translation key whose segment is a reserved name followed by the keySeparator (e.g. '__proto__.polluted', 'constructor.prototype.x') — the exact dotted bypass of the <=3.9.6 literal denylist that i18next-http-middleware's missingKeyHandler passes to i18next-fs-backend's unguarded setPath(). Article-specific: the '(__proto__|constructor|prototype).' segment shape is the CVE-2026-48714 payload signature, not a generic prototype-pollution template. Rationale: Uses the article's exact bypass string — a reserved segment (__proto__/constructor/prototype) followed by the default '.' keySeparator — which the 3.9.3 literal denylist misses. Legit i18next keys ('header.title') never start a segment with these names, so the '(reserved).' regex is high-fidelity; %2e branch catches URL-encoded delivery. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49m-vf83-692w • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48714 • https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-middleware/commit/7c6d26f137d3e940b8d229ca148bca38845faf49
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal DAST/vuln scanner (Burp, Nessus, ZAP) fuzzing the app with __proto__ payloads
  • Security research / red-team validation traffic against a staging host
  • A backend that legitimately uses a dotted key literally containing the word 'constructor' as free text (rare)
  • WAF that reflects the offending payload into its own alert Message field, double-counting the same request
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL has "/locales/add/" or Message has "/locales/add/" or RequestContext has "/locales/add/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request from the WAF/proxy log — confirm the payload targets '/locales/add/<lng>/<ns>' and that the segment is a reserved name + '.', then check whether the request returned 2xx (delivered) vs blocked. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF and, if missingKeyHandler is exposed unauthenticated, disable the route or set saveMissing:false immediately; verify the app runs i18next-http-middleware >=3.9.7 and i18next-fs-backend >=2.6.6. 3) Hunt: search for the same source IP hitting other endpoints, look for post-request app crashes/500s or anomalous auth-bypass behaviour indicating successful Object.prototype pollution, and review whether persisted locale files were modified.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__","constructor","prototype") or Message has_any ("__proto__","constructor","prototype") or RequestContext has_any ("__proto__","constructor","prototype")
| where (RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(__proto__|constructor|prototype)(\.|%2e)")
     or (Message matches regex @"(?i)(__proto__|constructor|prototype)(\.|%2e)")
     or (RequestContext matches regex @"(?i)(__proto__|constructor|prototype)(\.|%2e)")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: f49a1c2e-8b73-4d61-9a2f-6928b7f4c883
status: experimental
description: Detects a web request whose translation key contains a reserved segment (__proto__/constructor/prototype) immediately followed by the i18next keySeparator, the dotted bypass exploited in CVE-2026-48714 against i18next-http-middleware <=3.9.6 backed by i18next-fs-backend <=2.6.5.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49m-vf83-692w
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48714
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    c-uri|re: '(?i)(__proto__|constructor|prototype)(\.|%2e)'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate dotted translation keys never begin a segment with a reserved prototype name; internal DAST/security scanners probing the endpoint.
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*__proto__.*" OR Web.url="*constructor.*" OR Web.url="*prototype.*" OR Web.uri_query="*__proto__.*" OR Web.uri_query="*constructor.*" OR Web.uri_query="*prototype.*" OR Web.url="*__proto__%2e*" OR Web.url="*prototype%2e*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.uri_path Web.url Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*__proto__.*" OR Web.url="*constructor.*" OR Web.url="*prototype.*" OR Web.uri_query="*__proto__.*" OR Web.uri_query="*constructor.*" OR Web.uri_query="*prototype.*" OR Web.url="*__proto__%2e*" OR Web.url="*prototype%2e*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.uri_path Web.url Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Unauthenticated external POST to i18next missingKey route /locales/add/ (CVE-2026-48714 exposure) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces the CVE-2026-48714 attack surface directly: anonymous, external-source POST requests to the i18next-http-middleware default missing-key route '/locales/add/<lng>/<ns>'. This catches exposure and probing even when the WAF does not log request bodies, keying on the advisory's core precondition — missingKeyHandler reachable by untrusted input. Rationale: Pivots on the corroborated default missing-key route ('POST /locales/add/:lng/:ns') plus an external, non-RFC1918 source — the exact 'missingKeyHandler exposed to untrusted input' condition the advisory says makes an app exploitable. Route-based so it works even without request-body capture. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-middleware • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49m-vf83-692w • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48714
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A reverse proxy / CDN egress IP mis-classified as external while forwarding legitimate app missing-key writes
  • Client-side i18next instances with saveMissing enabled genuinely posting missing keys from real users
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring probing the locale endpoints
  • Internal QA reachable via a public load-balancer VIP that NATs the source to a public IP
Suppression filter
| where csUserName == "-" and cIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target host actually runs i18next-http-middleware and whether missingKeyHandler/saveMissing is enabled and reachable without auth; review the posting IPs' reputation and request volume. 2) Contain: put the '/locales/add/' route behind authentication or remove it, or set saveMissing:false; upgrade middleware to >=3.9.7 and i18next-fs-backend to >=2.6.6. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these source IPs against UC1 (dotted __proto__ payloads) to distinguish benign missing-key writes from pollution attempts, and inspect persisted namespace JSON files for injected __proto__/constructor keys.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "/locales/add/"
| where ipv4_is_private(cIP) == false
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 8), Paths = make_set(csUriStem, 8) by cIP, sSiteName, Computer
| order by Requests desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as requests min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.uri_path) as uri_paths from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.uri_path="*/locales/add/*" by Web.src Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | search NOT (src=10.0.0.0/8 OR src=172.16.0.0/12 OR src=192.168.0.0/16 OR src=127.0.0.0/8) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - requests
| tstats summariesonly=false count as requests min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents values(Web.uri_path) as uri_paths from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.uri_path="*/locales/add/*" by Web.src Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | search NOT (src=10.0.0.0/8 OR src=172.16.0.0/12 OR src=192.168.0.0/16 OR src=127.0.0.0/8) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - requests

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Gamaredon in 2025: Leveraging tunnels, workers, dead drops, and new alliances

ESET WeLiveSecurity

ESET Research analyzes Gamaredon’s new toolset and the group’s growing reliance on legitimate online services to hide its C&amp;C infrastructure and exfiltrate stolen data

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gamaredon HTA downloader auto-executing from Startup folder at logon (mshta.exe) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal dropping HTA/VBS into Startup folder · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Gamaredon dead-drop C&C resolution via Telegra.ph and GoFile from script hosts · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Gamaredon stealer exfiltration to S3-compatible cloud storage (Wasabi/Tebi/Intercolo) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal dropping HTA/VBS into Startup folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step Gamaredon adopted from 2025-09-26: a malicious RAR archive exploiting WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 (alternate-data-stream path traversal) to write an HTA/VBS/VBE/LNK downloader into the user's Startup folder so it auto-runs at next login. Article-specific because it pins the writing process to WinRAR-family binaries and the target to the Startup directory. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete persistence pivot (CVE-2025-8088 → HTA/VBS into Startup folder, active from 2025-09-26) and the WinRAR extraction binaries; Mandiant/Google and SOC Prime confirm the same ADS-to-Startup write pattern (.hta/.vbs/.vbe) across multiple Russia-aligned actors, so it is second-sourced. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability • https://socprime.com/active-threats/cve-2025-8088-critical-winrar-vulnerability/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/winrar-path-traversal-flaw-still-exploited-by-numerous-hackers/amp/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1203 T1564.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate installers shipped as RAR self-extractors that legitimately add a startup launcher
  • IT-deployed login scripts (.vbs/.lnk) packaged in archives by an admin
  • Software that bundles an updater shortcut into Startup after archive extraction
  • Security/portable apps extracted with WinRAR that create a startup auto-run by design
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/sfx","setup","install") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the dropped file's full path/hash and the parent RAR archive; detonate or read the HTA/VBS content for a download URL and confirm WinRAR version < 7.13 on the host. 2) Contain: delete/quarantine the Startup-folder artifact, isolate the host before next logon (the payload fires at login), and block any URLs/domains found in the script. 3) Hunt: search the org for the same archive SHA256 in mail/download telemetry, for other hosts running unpatched WinRAR, and for follow-on mshta/wscript execution and connections to telegra.ph / gofile.io / S3 storage domains.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".vbe" or FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("hta","vbs","vbe","lnk")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Script Drop into Startup Folder
id: a3f8c1d2-4b6e-4f21-9c7a-1e2d3f4a5b6c
description: Detects WinRAR-family process writing an HTA/VBS/VBE/LNK file into the user Startup folder, consistent with CVE-2025-8088 path-traversal persistence used by Gamaredon in 2025.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.t1547.001
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1564.004
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\unrar.exe'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.hta'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.vbe'
      - '.lnk'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_path and selection_ext
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\WinRAR.exe OR *\winrar.exe OR *\Rar.exe OR *\rar.exe OR *\UnRAR.exe OR *\unrar.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\Startup\*.hta OR *\Startup\*.vbs OR *\Startup\*.vbe OR *\Startup\*.lnk)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|rar|unrar)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\.+\.(hta|vbs|vbe|lnk)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Gamaredon HTA downloader auto-executing from Startup folder at logon (mshta.exe) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the persisted Gamaredon HTA downloader: mshta.exe launched at user logon with a command line referencing an .hta inside the Startup folder. Complements the file-write detection by catching execution even when the original drop was missed. Rationale: Pins to the article's specific persistence-to-execution chain (HTA downloader placed in Startup executes at next login) and the LOLBin mshta with a Startup-path command line, a combination with near-zero legitimate occurrence; corroborated by Google/Mandiant noting HTA-in-Startup as the second-stage downloader. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1547.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legacy in-house HTA-based dashboard intentionally placed in Startup by IT
  • Vendor application that uses an HTA splash/launcher auto-started at logon
  • Admin troubleshooting that temporarily drops an HTA in Startup
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the mshta command line and the referenced .hta path; read the HTA body for embedded URLs/next-stage (PteroSand VBScript) and check whether a RAR/CVE-2025-8088 drop preceded it. 2) Contain: kill the mshta process, remove the Startup artifact, isolate the host, and block extracted C2/dead-drop domains. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/host for child wscript/cscript execution, temporary .vbs written-then-deleted (PteroDum), and egress to telegra.ph, gofile.io, or S3 storage providers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".hta"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has ".hta"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HTA Downloader Executing from Startup Folder via mshta
id: b4e9d2c3-5c7f-4a32-8d6b-2f3e4a5b6c7d
description: Detects mshta.exe executing an HTA file located in the user Startup folder, consistent with Gamaredon CVE-2025-8088 logon persistence.

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="mshta.exe" AND Processes.process="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" AND Processes.process="*.hta*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Gamaredon stealer exfiltration to S3-compatible cloud storage (Wasabi/Tebi/Intercolo) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts PteroVDoor/PteroPSDoor's 2025 primary exfiltration channel: scripted upload of stolen files to S3-compatible storage at wasabisys.com, tebi.io, or i3storage.com (Intercolo de-fra.i3storage.com) initiated by a script host rather than a browser. High-fidelity because exfil from wscript/powershell/mshta to these specific providers is anomalous. Rationale: Uses the corroborated exfil endpoints (Wasabi=wasabisys.com, Tebi=tebi.io, Intercolo=de-fra.i3storage.com) named as Gamaredon's 2025 primary exfil channel, scoped to script-host initiators to suppress normal browser/backup S3 traffic; ESET's own write-up and the search-confirmed config-rotation (Wasabi→Tebi→Intercolo) second-source the domains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://www.govinfosecurity.com/russias-gamaredon-adapts-tactics-to-target-ukraine-a-32068
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1059.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate backup/sync software legitimately using Wasabi S3 (but normally via its own binary, not wscript/powershell)
  • Developer/DevOps PowerShell scripts pushing artifacts to a sanctioned Wasabi/Tebi bucket
  • A red-team or admin ad-hoc PowerShell aws/s3 upload
  • Telemetry where a browser helper is misattributed as the initiating process
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws s3","Backup","veeam") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("backupsvc","svc-backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating script host, its command line, and the volume/bytes uploaded; confirm the bucket/host is not a sanctioned corporate storage account. 2) Contain: block the storage FQDNs at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and preserve the stealer binary/script for analysis. 3) Hunt: trace back to the persistence/execution chain (mshta-from-Startup, WinRAR drop), enumerate which files were staged/read prior to upload, and sweep other hosts for DNS to the same three providers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("wasabisys.com","tebi.io","i3storage.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("wasabisys.com","tebi.io","i3storage.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon dead-drop C&C resolution via Telegra.ph and GoFile from script hosts AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts PteroOdd (Telegra.ph API) and PteroEffigy (GoFile) fetching next-stage payloads / resolving C&C from legitimate dead-drop services, requested by a Windows script host. Article-specific because it targets the exact two services named for these downloaders rather than generic LOLBin egress. Rationale: Targets the two specific dead-drop services the article ties to named downloaders (PteroOdd→Telegra.ph API, PteroEffigy→GoFile) and scopes to script-host initiators so normal browser visits to telegra.ph/gofile are excluded; flagged Medium because only the original ESET piece names these two services for these tools. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately downloading a shared file from gofile.io that an EDR attributes to a script wrapper
  • Automation/scripts that scrape telegra.ph articles for benign content
  • Browser child processes mis-tagged as the initiating process
  • Security tooling sandboxing a URL that resolves these domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the script-host command line and the full URL/telegra.ph path or gofile content ID; pull what was downloaded and decode any retrieved next-stage C&C address. 2) Contain: block telegra.ph/gofile.io egress from the host, isolate it, and add the resolved real C&C to blocklists. 3) Hunt: correlate with preceding HTA/mshta execution and following uploads to wasabisys.com/tebi.io/i3storage.com on the same host, and sweep the org for other script hosts touching these dead-drop services.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("telegra.ph","gofile.io")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("telegra.ph","gofile.io")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    category: file_access

detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'

        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

            - '\chrome.exe'

level: high
